meta.title: Decision register — questions, information, answers
meta.purpose: Every question that must be answered before a product, model or staking decision can reasonably be made, plus what we already know, what we do not know, and the cheapest action that closes each gap.

status_values.answered: Closed with an official source or with arithmetic reproduced by a script in this repo.
status_values.partial: Partially closed: some evidence exists but it does not support a decision on its own.
status_values.unknown: No evidence. A decision that depends on this is not decision-ready.
status_values.blocked: Cannot be closed by research alone; needs a purchase, a legal opinion, or a human decision.

priority_values.P0: Hard blocker — nothing downstream is valid without it.

meta.answered_count_note: Counts are generated by scripts/build_site.py from this file; nothing is stated here that the file does not contain.

questions.question: Under what terms may this project store and display NFL data, and does a public GitHub Pages site fall inside those terms?
questions.why: The site publishes 32 clubs' records, 108 injury rows and player links. If redistribution is outside the terms of use, the public site is the problem, not the model.
questions.blocks: Any public publication; the entire hosting decision.
questions.current_answer: Not answered. No terms-of-use document was fetched and no licence was reviewed in this session.
questions.evidence: nfl.com and operations.nfl.com pages were fetched and quoted; no licence text was read.
questions.how_to_close: Read the NFL.com Terms of Use and the NFL.com privacy/usage pages; record the clauses that govern republication of statistics. If unclear, restrict the public site to derived analysis (ratios, indices, model output) and keep raw rows behind a summary. Get a written opinion before scaling.

questions.question: Is a stable, machine-readable official injury feed available, and at what cost?
questions.why: The requirement is 'no manual input'. Today the extract was assembled by reading rendered HTML, which does not scale and will drift.
questions.current_answer: Partial. The official report exists as a rendered page (S05) and is fetchable, but no documented programmatic endpoint was confirmed.
questions.evidence: S05 returns clean per-player rows in page text; 108 rows were transcribed without ambiguity.
questions.how_to_close: Probe for a documented JSON endpoint or a licensed data vendor (official NFL data partners). Until then, pin the parser to the page structure and alert on row-count drift.

questions.question: Which official source is authoritative for player-level performance (snaps, routes, targets, carries)?
questions.why: Player props cannot be originated without usage data. Team totals alone cannot support a prop model.
questions.current_answer: Unknown. No stats page was fetched in this session, so no claim is made about what it contains.
questions.evidence: None gathered.
questions.how_to_close: Fetch the official NFL stats surfaces, confirm which fields are published and at what granularity, and record the exact URL per field before any prop model is specified.

questions.question: Where does a historical archive of closing lines and prices come from?
questions.why: Skill in this domain is measured against the closing line. Without a line archive there is no CLV, no ATS record, no backtest, and no way to separate skill from luck.
questions.blocks: Every validation gate from G2 onward. The entire leaderboard.
questions.current_answer: Not answered, and the official-source route is closed: nfl.com/odds/ returns 404 (S09), and NFL Support (S13) confirms that the odds on NFL surfaces are partner-bookmaker numbers with no archive.
questions.evidence: S13: 'the NFL widgets show odds, spreads, and over/under number provided by official bookmaker partners of the NFL (FanDuel, Caesars, and DraftKings)'. Lines are a sportsbook product, not a league product.
questions.how_to_close: Choose a commercial odds archive (paid), then define 'closing line' precisely (which book, which timestamp, snapshot rule). This is a purchase decision, not a research task.

questions.question: Is betting on NFL markets legal for the operator in the jurisdiction of residence?
questions.why: The leaderboard pays rewards for performance. If the activity is not lawful where the operator lives, the reward structure must not be built.
questions.blocks: Reward design, staking, and any real-money linkage.
questions.current_answer: Unknown. No regulatory source was consulted in this session and none is asserted.
questions.evidence: None. Deliberately left blank rather than assumed.
questions.how_to_close: Obtain a written legal opinion for the operator's jurisdiction covering: personal betting, publishing selections, and paying performance rewards. Do not rely on a blog post or a forum.

questions.question: What is the true cost of a bet — i.e. what is the achievable price, not the advertised one?
questions.why: Edge is price-dependent. A 54% win rate is profitable at -105 and unprofitable at -115.
questions.blocks: Stake sizing, ROI gates, and every EV calculation.
questions.current_answer: Unknown. No price data of any kind was collected.
questions.evidence: None.
questions.how_to_close: Record the actual available price at decision time for every simulated bet, including line movement and limits. Store it, do not estimate it later.

questions.question: What exactly counts as a graded bet, and how are pushes, voids, and line moves graded?
questions.why: A leaderboard is only as honest as its grading. Retro-grading against a line you picked after the fact is the most common way these competitions lie to themselves.
questions.current_answer: Partial. A grading spec is proposed on the Strategy page; it is a proposal, not a verified standard.
questions.evidence: Proposed rules: bet is graded at the price recorded at submission; pushes refund; a line move does not re-grade a bet.
questions.how_to_close: Adopt the spec in writing before the first bet is logged, with an immutable timestamp on every submission.

questions.question: Does the baseline rating beat a naive benchmark out of sample?
questions.why: A model that cannot beat 'home team by 2.5' is not a signal. This is the first honest test.
questions.blocks: Any promotion of the model to a strategy.
questions.current_answer: Not answered. It cannot be answered without a game log and a line archive.
questions.evidence: The engine is built and runs (scripts/model_ratings.py) but has never seen a historical line.
questions.how_to_close: Ingest game-level results (scores by week) to compute opponent-adjusted ratings, then walk-forward test against the closing line. Weekly game pages exist (S06) and are the unblocking step.

questions.question: Where does the official depth order (1st / 2nd / 3rd string) come from?
questions.why: The core requirement — knowing when 2nd/3rd/4th string players replace starters — is exactly a depth-order question. Injury designations alone cannot answer it.
questions.blocks: The entire backup-deficiency feature, on both offence and defence.
questions.current_answer: Partially answered, and the answer is negative for the obvious route: the official NFL.com roster page exposes position and roster status but has no depth-order column (R14).
questions.evidence: S07 was read in full: the table columns are player, number, position, status, height, weight, experience, college. No depth rank.
questions.how_to_close: Two candidate routes to evaluate: (a) per-club official depth-chart pages (each club publishes its own; not machine-readable and not uniform), (b) derive depth from snap counts if an official snap-count source exists. Both must be verified per club before any 'starter' claim is published.

questions.question: How much is a missing starter actually worth in points, by position?
questions.why: Without a value per position, an injury list cannot be turned into a line adjustment. This is the difference between a dashboard and a model.
questions.current_answer: Unknown and currently an explicit assumption (A-04) with weights declared in scripts/model_ratings.py.
questions.evidence: No official source publishes position-value weights. The weights used are labelled assumptions and are not presented as measured.
questions.how_to_close: Estimate empirically: regress closing-line movement (or realised margin) on verified availability changes, with enough events to control for opponent. Requires Q-04 first.

questions.question: When in the week is the game status actually knowable?
questions.why: A line originated before the status is published is a guess about information that does not yet exist. The timing defines the tradable window.
questions.current_answer: Partial. Evidence from the live page: on Thursday, only 6 of 108 listed players carried a game status.
questions.evidence: 108 rows captured, 6 with Out/Questionable. The rest are practice-report-only, which is consistent with the league scheme (R01/R02) but the exact publication deadline is unverified (R05).
questions.how_to_close: Snapshot the same page on Friday and Saturday and diff it. That yields the published-deadline behaviour empirically instead of from secondary claims.

questions.question: What form do rewards take, and what prevents the reward from paying for luck?
questions.why: 'Rewards for top performing strategies' is the stated design. If ranking is on raw profit, the winner is usually the luckiest.
questions.current_answer: Partial. A design exists: hard gates must all pass, then ranking is on a shrunk, out-of-sample composite rather than raw ROI (Strategy page).
questions.evidence: Scoring formula and gates are specified and reproducible in scripts/strategy_gates.py.
questions.how_to_close: Human decision on the reward currency (money, allocation, privileges) and on the minimum evaluation period. Lawful-status question Q-05 must close first.

questions.question: How large a sample is needed before a strategy is allowed to claim an edge?
questions.why: This is the numeric heart of 'remove luck'. Without it, a 12-3 start looks like skill.
questions.current_answer: Answered as a method. Gate G1 requires a pre-registered minimum n derived from the effect size you claim to detect, with a 3.0 t-statistic floor and bootstrap confirmation.
questions.evidence: scripts/strategy_gates.py implements the sample-size calculation and prints the required n for a grid of edges.
questions.how_to_close: Nothing further to research; the operator must choose the target edge, which sets n mechanically.

questions.question: What are the real correlations between legs, rather than assumed ones?
questions.why: Parlay and same-game-parlay pricing lives or dies on the joint probability. Treating correlated legs as independent is the single fastest way to lose money while believing you have an edge.
questions.current_answer: Unknown empirically. The *method* is answered (Gaussian copula on leg-level outcomes, implemented in scripts/parlay_math.py) but no leg-level dataset exists to estimate rho.
questions.evidence: Only cross-sectional team correlations could be computed (C1-C8). Those are not leg correlations.
questions.how_to_close: Build a leg-level outcomes table (player-game and team-game results) and estimate pairwise rho by cluster. Until then no parlay is priced.

questions.question: Which signals survive once multiple testing is priced in?
questions.why: Testing 200 ideas at p<0.05 yields ~10 'discoveries' by chance. A leaderboard that ignores this rewards the search, not the edge.
questions.blocks: Admission of any strategy to the leaderboard.
questions.current_answer: Answered as a method. Gate G5 applies a deflated Sharpe / Bonferroni-style correction using the number of variants actually tried, which must be logged.
questions.evidence: scripts/strategy_gates.py
questions.how_to_close: Operational requirement: log every variant tried, including failures. The correction is only valid if the trial count is honest.

questions.question: What bankroll, what fraction, and what drawdown limit?
questions.why: Kelly is only optimal if the edge estimate is right; it is savage when it is wrong. A leaderboard without a ruin constraint selects for reckless sizing.
questions.current_answer: Unknown. No bankroll is defined and none is assumed.
questions.evidence: None. The site deliberately publishes no stake sizes.
questions.how_to_close: Human decision: bankroll unit, maximum fraction per bet, maximum daily exposure, and a hard stop rule. Then encode fractional Kelly with a cap.

questions.question: Does the model's own total (points) estimate beat the naive average, and by how much?
questions.why: The two totals estimators published here disagree by up to 12 points on the same game (MIN@GB: 39.0 vs 51.2). A 12-point disagreement is not a small modelling detail.
questions.current_answer: Partial, and deliberately surfaced. Both estimators are published side by side with the disagreement flagged rather than hidden.
questions.evidence: scripts/model_ratings.py output for the eight verified Week 10 games.
questions.how_to_close: Score both estimators against realised totals from game logs, walk-forward. Whichever wins becomes the headline.

questions.question: How does a value get into a table, and what stops an unverified value from being published?
questions.why: The requirement is explicit: no hallucinated values, blanks stay blank and are flagged.
questions.blocks: Trust in every table on the site.
questions.current_answer: Answered as a mechanism. Every row carries a source id that must resolve to an official URL; the build fails if a row has no source. Unverified fields are null and render as '—' plus a flag.
questions.evidence: scripts/verify.py enforces: source id exists, source is official or explicitly marked secondary, no numeric field present without a source, no broken internal link.
questions.how_to_close: Nothing further; the gate must simply keep running on every build.

questions.question: Are there internal contradictions inside the official data itself?
questions.why: If the official source contradicts itself, a downstream model inherits the contradiction.
questions.blocks: Nothing, but it changes how much rounding/precision is defensible.
questions.current_answer: Answered for the standings snapshot: all four integrity checks pass, but squad games-played are unequal (8 vs 9) because of byes and the in-progress slate.
questions.evidence: scripts/verify.py check_integrity() reproduces: W+L+T = home+road; division subset of conference; conference + other-conference = total; PF-PA = published NET for all 32 clubs.
questions.how_to_close: Closed.

questions.question: Is the 'Questionable' label informative enough to trade on?
questions.why: Questionable means 'uncertain' by rule (R02). If the label has no calibration, any model feature built on it is noise.
questions.current_answer: Unknown. The rule is verified; the empirical play-rate of Questionable players is not measured here.
questions.evidence: Only 6 designated players in this week's extract — far too few to calibrate anything.
questions.how_to_close: Accumulate several seasons of designations joined to actual participation (inactive lists), then measure the play rate per designation. Report with confidence intervals.

questions.question: Can the final inactive list be captured before kickoff?
questions.why: The inactive list is the last word on availability. Anything before it is a probability, not a fact.
questions.current_answer: Unknown. No inactive-list surface was fetched in this session.
questions.evidence: None.
questions.how_to_close: Locate the official inactive announcement surface and timestamp it relative to kickoff.

questions.question: Is the fitted Pythagorean exponent stable, or is it fitting noise at n=32?
questions.why: The exponent was estimated at 3.51 from a 32-row snapshot. A parameter estimated from 32 points is not a law.
questions.blocks: Using the luck table as a betting input.
questions.current_answer: Partial. Reported with its residual error and explicitly described as snapshot-fitted.
questions.evidence: k=3.51 minimises SSE over the 32 clubs; the classic value quoted in public analytics is lower, which is itself a warning about small-sample fit.
questions.how_to_close: Re-fit weekly and plot the estimate over time. Only trust it once it is stable across weeks and across seasons.

questions.question: Can the site be rebuilt and verified without a human in the loop?
questions.why: The requirement is no manual input.
questions.current_answer: Partial. Build and verification are scripted (scripts/build_site.py, scripts/verify.py) but data ingestion for injuries is still a manual transcription step in this session.
questions.evidence: Two scripts plus a single command rebuild the entire site from JSON.
questions.how_to_close: Replace manual transcription with a parser plus a drift alarm; keep the human only as the approver of flagged values.

questions.question: What stops a strategy from being overfitted to the leaderboard itself?
questions.why: If the same people both tune and rank, the leaderboard becomes a fitting target.
questions.current_answer: Answered as a mechanism: pre-registration of the rule, a locked holdout, and a trial log; G4 requires walk-forward only.
questions.evidence: scripts/strategy_gates.py G4/G5.
questions.how_to_close: Operational discipline: freeze a rule before it sees data.

questions.question: Which single source is authoritative when two official pages disagree?
questions.why: A conflict protocol prevents silent cherry-picking.
questions.blocks: Nothing yet; prevents future silent errors.
questions.current_answer: Answered as a policy: the more specific page wins (player page over team page over league page); if still conflicting, publish both and flag.
questions.evidence: Applied once in this build: club page record (S08) agreed with league standings (S01); practice-squad size conflict (I-06) was flagged instead of resolved.
questions.how_to_close: Closed.
